title: They Dreamed of Going Home to Iran. Then the Bombs Fell.
excerpt: Iranian Americans who had planned to visit or return to their homeland now face an agonizing reality: a war with no clear end and family they cannot reach.
body:
• Iranian Americans who once planned to return home are now torn between hope for regime change and fear for family caught in the crossfire
  • Communication with relatives in Iran remains difficult months into the war, with phone and internet connections unreliable
  • A deep split has emerged within the diaspora over whether U.S. military intervention can deliver democracy or will only deepen suffering

When the United States and Israel launched strikes on Iran on February 28, millions of Iranian Americans found themselves glued to their screens, some clinging to hope it might bring a brighter future to their homeland, others terrified their relatives would suffer in a war with no certain end.

For many in the diaspora, the initial hours brought a complicated kind of euphoria. Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who had ruled Iran for decades while violently crushing dissent, was killed early in the attack. In Los Angeles — home to the largest Iranian expatriate community in the United States — some popped Champagne, some downed shots of tequila, and some took to the streets.

“We are happy that he is gone and he can’t kill our innocent people anymore.”

— Ava Farhadi, 33, postdoctoral researcher in Indiana

Farhadi’s family participated in the massive anti-government protests in January, which were met with a brutal crackdown that killed thousands. While her immediate family was unhurt, friends and close loved ones were among those killed when security forces opened fire on peaceful demonstrators.

Hope Turned to Anguish

But the initial euphoria has given way to something far darker. Months into the conflict, the ceasefire reached in June has collapsed into daily attacks and counterattacks. Eighteen U.S. service members have been killed, thousands of Iranians are dead, and oil prices have surged, adding to inflation pressures globally.

For Iranians inside the country, the reality is grinding. Somayeh, a 40-year-old photographer in Tehran, told Reuters her weekly grocery prices had nearly doubled since the war began. “The most important thing overall in the middle of the war is the economy. Every day our situation is worse and more difficult,” she said. “We can’t even make plans for two days in the future.”

Somayeh had once planned to leave Iran. Now she says she would not go even if she could. “My life, home and family are here. Even if I was able to leave for a few months, I’d have to return and continue my life here.”

A Diaspora Divided

A deep fault line has emerged among the estimated 5 to 10 million Iranians living abroad. At a rally in Toronto in late April, around 300 protesters waved U.S. and Israeli flags and called for continued military action to topple the theocratic government. “The Islamic regime is our main enemy. We want countries like the U.S. and Israel to help us bring this regime down,” said Ali Daneshfar of Cyrus the Great, a Toronto-based Iranian group.

Others sharply disagree. Nasser Sharif, president of the California Society for Democracy in Iran, warned that bombing only strengthens the authorities’ grip. “The regime is using the war to suppress more, execute more people and terrorize the population inside the country,” he said.

Writer and translator Maryam Raeesdana captured the shift in sentiment. “The Iranian people had hope — maybe help is coming. But after one week, two weeks, three weeks, they lost it day by day, bomb after bomb,” she told NPR.

They Don’t Want to Leave Home

Inside Iran, people who once considered emigrating now find themselves unable to leave — and, paradoxically, determined to stay. Amir, a 30-year-old software engineer in Sanandaj, married shortly before the war began. Internet outages destroyed his remote work. He spent months with crippling debt before finding a job only days ago.

Yet he refuses to leave. “My mom was around during the Iran-Iraq War and she said my grandfather would say that it’s OK if we died, as long as we were under our own roof,” he said. “We don’t want to leave our home.”

Nazanin, a 34-year-old psychotherapist in Sanandaj, said the plummeting rial has made emigrating financially impossible. But she said it was worry about her family during airstrikes that ultimately changed her mind. “The thought of not being with them and of having the destiny of a person living alone with grief was so difficult that it impacted my idea of emigrating.”

Waiting for a Plane That May Never Come

In the United States, the ache of separation persists. Gita Zarnegar, a 63-year-old psychoanalyst whose Jewish family left Iran in 1979, said she would visit the moment it was safe. “I will be the first person on that plane,” she said.

But for many, that plane feels further away than ever. Alborz Pakravan, who works in the semiconductor industry in Arizona, described his mother’s reaction when the ceasefire was first announced: she cried as she had never cried before. “She was really disappointed,” he told NPR. “She said, we are being played. She said, damn this Donald Trump because he betrayed us.”

The war has entered its sixth month with no diplomatic resolution in sight. For Iranian Americans caught between two countries, the question is no longer when they will go home — but whether home, as they remember it, will still exist when the fighting stops.
nri_angle: Iranian Americans who dreamed of returning to their homeland are now divided over whether the U.S. war with Iran will deliver the democratic change they sought or destroy the home they longed to return to.
author: Diaspora Desk
